Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 3:

﴿In the nearest land﴾. It is said: it is the Jazirah (the Mesopotamian upper land), which lies between al-Sham and Iraq, and it is the nearest land of the Romans to Persia. And it is said: it is the nearest land of the Arabs to them, namely the borders of al-Sham. ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾. **Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 30, Verse 4:**

﴿In a few years.﴾ *Al-bid'* (a few) refers to the number between three and nine.

﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice.﴾ It is narrated that the victory of the Romans over the Persians occurred on the day of Badr. It is also said that it occurred on the day of Hudaybiyyah, so the believers rejoiced at the victory of God for them over the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is also said that the believers rejoiced at the victory of the Romans over the Persians, because the Romans were *Ahl al-Kitab* (People of the Scripture), so they were closer to Islam. Likewise, the disbelievers of Quraysh rejoiced at the victory of the Persians over the Romans, because the Persians were not People of the Scripture, so they were closer to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

It is narrated that when the disbelievers rejoiced at this, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) went out to them and said: "Our Prophet (ﷺ) has informed us from Allah, Exalted is He, that they will certainly be defeated." He made a wager with them for ten *qalus* (the plural of *qalus*, which is a young she-camel) to be paid within three years. This was before gambling (*qimar*) was prohibited. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Increase the stake for them and extend the term for them." So he made the *qalus* one hundred, and the term nine years. Ubayy ibn Khalaf also made a similar wager with him. When the matter came to pass as he had reported, Abu Bakr took the *qalus* from the descendants of Ubayy ibn Khalaf, since he had died. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "Give them in charity."

"Promise of Allah" (wa'd Allah) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid), like your saying: "I owe him a thousand dirhams, acknowledged" ('urfan), because its meaning is: "I have acknowledged to him that they are his."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 7:

﴿They know the outward appearance of the worldly life﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that they know what is perceived by the senses, but not what is perceived by the intellect; in this they are like the beasts. It has also been said: "the outward" is what is known through observation by the first principles of reason, and "the inward" is what is known through reflection and proof. It has been said: it derives from "zuhur" in the sense of elevation, meaning worldly (superiority). It has also been said: "zahir" means that which is transient and passes away. The most apparent view is that by "the outward" He meant knowledge of worldly affairs and their benefits, because He described them afterwards as heedless of the Hereafter, and that requires their lack of knowledge of it. Consider how He first denied them knowledge, then affirmed for them knowledge of the worldly life alone. Some scholars of rhetoric said: this is an antithesis (muṭābaqa) due to the combination of negation and affirmation. Some of them considered the affirmed knowledge as though it were nonexistent because of its scant benefit, so on this view it is an explanation of the negation.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾

This may have two meanings. The first is that "themselves" (al-nafs) is the place of the reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth, as if he said: "Have they not reflected with their minds, so that they would know that God did not create the heavens and the earth except with truth?" The second is that the meaning is: have they not reflected upon their own selves and their creation, so that they might infer from that the Creator? In this case, his words "He did not create..." (ma khalaqa, the verse that follows) would be a resumption of speech (isti'naf). The first meaning is more apparent.
﴿And they plowed the earth﴾, i.e., they tilled it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 10:

﴿Then the final outcome of those who did evil was the worst (outcome)﴾. The meaning of al-Su'a (the worst): the destruction of the disbelievers. The word al-Su'a is the feminine of al-Asw'a (the worst), just as al-Husna is the feminine of al-Ahsan (the best). The word ʿāqibah (outcome) has been read in the nominative (ʿāqibatu), in which case it is the subject of kāna (was), and al-Su'a is its predicate. It has also been read in the accusative (ʿāqibata), in which case it is the predicate of kāna, and al-Su'a is its subject. The phrase inna kadhdhabū (because they denied) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi), meaning "because they denied." It is also possible that al-Su'a is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of asā'ū (they did evil).
﴿The guilty will be plunged into despair﴾. Iblas is being in a state of evil together with despair of any good.
﴿They will be separated﴾ means: into their abodes and their recompense.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 15:

﴿They will be made joyful﴾ — you will be made to enjoy delight, from al-hubur (ḥubūr), which is joy and bliss; and it has been said: you will be honored.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verses 17–18:

﴿So glory be to God﴾. This is a teaching for the servants, meaning: say "Glory be to God" when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, ﴿and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon time﴾, meaning when you enter the time of midday (al-zuhayra), which is the middle of the day. His saying, ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾, is an interjection between the coordinated clauses. It has also been said that by this He means the five daily prayers: ﴿when you enter the evening﴾ refers to the Maghrib and the 'Isha', ﴿when you enter the morning﴾ refers to the Subh (Fajr), ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ refers to the 'Asr, and ﴿when you enter the noon time﴾ refers to the Zuhr.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 25:

﴿That the heaven and the earth should stand firm by His command﴾ means: they remain established, or their management (tadbir) stands. ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾. "Idha" in the first occurrence is conditional (shartiyya), and the second "idha" is sudden (fuja'iyya), and it is the answer (jawab) of the first. The call (da'wa) in this verse is His saying to the dead: "Arise," by the second blast in the Trumpet (al-Sur). "Min al-ard" (from the earth) is connected either to His saying "mukhrijun" (you will be brought out) or to His saying "da'akum" (He calls you), on the basis that the point of origin (al-ghaya) is considered in relation to the one being called, like your saying: "I called you from the mountain," when the one called is on the mountain.
﴿قَانِتُونَ﴾ [all devoutly obedient] is mentioned in al-Baqarah [2:116].

Translation of the passage:

﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: that is, the restoration on the Day of Resurrection is easier for Him than the first creation. This is a way of bringing the matter closer to the understanding of the listener and of confirming the resurrection, for whoever makes a thing the first time finds it easier the second time. But all matters are equal with Allah, for indeed everything is easy for Allah. ﴿And to Him belongs the highest description﴾: that is, the highest attribute with which the people of the heavens and the earth describe Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 28:

﴿Is there for you, from among what your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal therein and fear them as you fear one another?﴾ This is the parable that is struck. Its meaning is: you, O people, do not have your slaves as partners in your wealth, nor are they equal to you in your circumstances. Likewise, God Most High has no partners among His servants in His dominion, and none is equal to Him in His lordship. The interrogative particle (hal) is mentioned, and its meaning is affirmation of a negation (al-taqrir ʿala al-nafy). Included in the negation is His saying: ﴿So you are equal in it, and you fear them as you fear your own selves﴾. That is: you are not equal with your slaves in your property, and you do not fear them as you fear free persons like yourselves, because slaves are, in your estimation, far less and more lowly than that.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 30, verse 29:

﴿Nay, those who did wrong follow their own desires﴾ The use of "bal" (nay, rather) here is a turning away (idrab) from what the preceding verse implied, as if to say: they have no proof for their associating partners with God; rather, they follow their desires in this without knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 30:

﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾ — it is the religion of Islam. Setting the face (iqamat al-wajh) in both places in the surah is an expression of turning toward it and being sincere in it, in His saying ﴿So set﴾. And ﴿al-qayyim﴾ is a kind of paronomasia (tajnis, a rhetorical device of close-sounding word play).

﴿The fitrah of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), like His saying: "the dye of Allah" (sibghat Allah), or as an object of a implied verb, its estimate being: "Adhere to the fitrah of Allah," or "upon you is the fitrah of Allah." Its meaning is the creation of Allah (khilqat Allah), and what is meant by it is the religion of Islam, because Allah created creation upon it, since it is what their sound intellects require. Whoever disbelieved did so only due to an external factor that removed him from the original of his fitrah, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian."

﴿There is no alteration to the creation of Allah﴾ means: by the creation of Allah is meant the fitrah upon which people were created, of faith. The meaning that Allah does not alter it is that He does not create people upon other than it; but the devils of mankind and jinn alter it after the first creation. Or the meaning is that people should not alter that fitrah, so the negation in this case is a command, not a report. It has also been said that it is specific to the believers; that is, there is no alteration of Allah's fitrah with regard to one whom Allah has decreed will remain steadfast in his faith. It has also been said that it is a prohibition against altering creation, such as castrating male animals, cutting off their ears, and the like.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 31:

﴿Turning back in repentance to Him﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of His words ﴿So set your face [upright for the religion]﴾, because the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, while the intended meaning is himself and his community. For this reason He addressed them in plural in His words "munībīna" (turning back in repentance). It was also said that it is a ḥāl of the implied subject pronoun in "ilzamū" (adhere to) in ﴿the fiṭrah of Allah﴾; and it was also said that it is a ḥāl of His words "faṭara al-nās" (He originated mankind), but this is far-fetched. ﴿And fear Him﴾ and what follows it are conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to "aqim wajhaka" (set your face), or to the governing element (al-'āmil) of "fiṭrat Allah", which is the implied "ilzamū" (adhere to).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 36:

﴿And when We let the people taste mercy﴾ This is a rebuke of those who rejoice and exult when good befalls them, and despair when evil befalls them. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 39:

﴿And whatever you give in usury so that it may increase within the wealth of people﴾ [etc.]: its meaning is like His saying: ﴿Allah eliminates usury and makes charities grow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], that is, whatever you give from your wealth in the manner of usury, it does not grow with Allah. As for what you give in charity (sadaqat), it is that which grows with Allah and benefits you thereby. It was also said: the intended meaning is that a man gives a gift to another man, or presents him with a gift, so that he may be compensated with more than that. This, although it is permissible, carries no reward.

It is also recited as ﴿وَمَآ آتَيْتُمْ﴾ with a long vowel (ātaytum), meaning "you gave" (a'taytum), and with a short vowel (ataytum), meaning "you came", i.e. you did it. ﴿لِّيَرْبُوَاْ﴾ is read with an upright ta' (litarbū) and ﴿لِّيَرْبُوَاْ﴾ with an open ya' and the waw in the accusative (liyarbuwā). ﴿فَأُوْلَـٰئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُضْعِفُونَ﴾ (fa-ulā'ika hum al-muḍ'ifūn): al-muḍ'if is the one who possesses multiplication (ih'āf) of good deeds. In this sentence there is a shift (iltifāt) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khiṭāb). The original form would have been: "And whatever you give of zakat, then you are the multipliers (al-muḍ'ifūn)." There is also an ellipsis in it, since a pronoun referring back to mā is necessary; its estimated form is "the multipliers through it," or "those who give it are the multipliers."

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 30, verses 48–49:**

﴿Then it stirs up clouds﴾: that is, moves them and spreads them out. ﴿In pieces﴾: that is, in fragments. It is also recited as كِسْفاً with the sin sukun (كِسْفاً), and both are two forms of the plural (بناءان للجمع). It was said that the meaning of the sukun form is that the cloud is one single piece. ﴿The rain﴾ is the water. ﴿From within it﴾: al-khilal (خلال) is the gap that lies between one part and another, since it is interspersed among its parts, and the pronoun refers back to the cloud. ﴿Before﴾ is repeated for emphasis, and to convey the speed with which people's hearts turn from despair to joy. ﴿Despairing﴾: that is, desperate, as in His saying: ﴿He sends down the rain after they had despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28].

The pronoun refers to the vegetation that God causes to grow by the rain, and the meaning is: if God sends a wind and the vegetation turns yellow because of it, people would disbelieve through despair and by objecting against God. It was said that the pronoun refers to the wind, and it was said that it refers to the clouds, but the first is better in meaning.

Verse: "So indeed you cannot make the dead hear" (﴿فَإِنَّكَ لاَ تُسْمِعُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ﴾) and so on: a metaphor (istiʿarah) for the unbelievers' failure to hear admonitions and proofs. He likened the unbelievers to the dead in their lack of perception.

﴿He created you from weakness﴾. The first weakness is that man is created from a despised fluid, and that he is weak in childhood. The second, the final weakness, is decrepitude (al-haram, extreme old age). It is recited with both the fatha and the damma on the ḍād in الضعف, and they are two dialects (lughatān) of the same word.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 55:

﴿They swore they had not remained [in the graves] but an hour﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and its meaning is that they swear they did not remain in the graves beneath the dust except for an hour, that is, they did not remain in the world except for an hour, and this is because that period seems short to them. ﴿Thus they were ever deluded﴾, meaning: in the same way they were turned away from truth and certainty in the world, until they would see things as they really are.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 30, verse 56:

﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say﴾: they are the angels, the prophets, and the believers. They refute the claim of the disbelievers which they swore to, ﴿"You remained [in the grave] according to the Decree of Allah"﴾. ﴿"In the Book of Allah"﴾ means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) or the knowledge of Allah. On this view, the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) is connected to his words ﴿"you remained"﴾. It was also said that it means the Qur'an. On this view, this prepositional phrase is connected to his words ﴿"were given knowledge"﴾, and there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence. Its meaning on this view is: "Those who were given knowledge in the Book of Allah," that is, the scholars of the Book of Allah, will say. Their words ﴿"Indeed you remained"﴾ are addressed to the disbelievers. Their words ﴿"So this is the Day of Resurrection"﴾ are a confirmation to them, and in meaning it is the answer to a presumed condition (shart muqaddar), whose sense is: "If you were denying the Resurrection, then this is the Day of Resurrection."

﴿Nor will they be granted the chance to make amends.﴾ *Al-'utbā* (من العتبى) derives from *al-'utba*, meaning *al-ridā* (satisfaction, pleasure). That is, ﴿wa-lā hum yusta'tabūn﴾ means: "and they will not be pleased." The *istaf'ala* form in *yusta'tabūn* (استفعل) is not used here to indicate seeking or requesting.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 30, verse 60:

﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾: meaning, the promise of victory over the disbelievers. ﴿And let not those who have no certainty make you unsteady﴾: from al-khiffah (lightness, unsteadiness), i.e., do not be agitated by their words.
